tagline.text: National Cultural Treasure church with a mermaid-and-seashell retablo

location.label: Location
location.text: Manila North Road, Magsingal, Ilocos Sur

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–800 (round-trip transport and snacks from Vigan, per person)

children.text: Standing in the heart of Magsingal in Ilocos Sur, this church was built in 1827 and declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2001. Its molave-wood retablo decorated with mermaids and seashells and the bell tower of the ruined old church are the main sights.

Magsingal Church is formally the Saint William the Hermit Parish (San Guillermo), and it sits right beside the Manila North Road, the national highway, in the town of Magsingal, Ilocos Sur. It lies about
11 km
north of Vigan, so it makes a good stop after exploring Vigan's historic district on your way north to Ilocos Norte. The church belongs to the Archdiocese of Nueva Segovia.

The history goes back to 1676, when Augustinian friars established the parish here. The first church was built in 1692 but was destroyed by an earthquake in 1723, and all that remains of the old church today is the bell tower and some wall fragments. The present church was built in 1827 and is the town's second church. Its three-storey facade, painted cream and white, is supported by the thick buttresses typical of Ilocos churches, giving it a sturdy, unpretentious look.

On July 31, 2001, the National Museum of the Philippines declared the church, its Baroque woodwork, convent, ruins, bell tower, school and Way of the Cross together a National Cultural Treasure. It is also one of the 26 Spanish colonial-era churches chosen by the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) for its conservation program. In December 2020, the National Museum completed the restoration and site improvement of the ruins, the bell tower and the surrounding grounds and handed the complex over to the Archdiocese of Nueva Segovia. The museum's director-general called it one of the great churches in the Philippines, praising its authenticity and its retablo.

This is not a large or flashy attraction. Instead, you can take your time in one compound with a retablo that feels like the sea brought indoors, a carved wooden pulpit, a brick bell tower and a museum in the old convent. One hour is enough, so it fits nicely into a Vigan day or a trip through northern Ilocos.

The church's greatest pride is its Baroque-style retablo made of molave wood. The topmost niche holds a statue of St. William with a mermaid on each side, the crown is a seashell, and the sides are filled with seahorses, waves and starfish. The way to appreciate it is to read the whole retablo as a seascape.

blocks.title: Molave Woodwork Said to Use No Nails

children.text: The retablo and the choir loft columns are made of hard molave wood, and tradition says no nails were used. The columns of the main altar are twisted Solomonic columns carved with plant motifs. You can see the grain and craftsmanship up close, which is why many photographers visit.

blocks.title: The Pulpit with the Boy and Horn

children.text: The pulpit carries a statue of a boy blowing a native horn (tambuli). It is said to have been made by Pablo Tamayo, a local fisherman who also designed the choir loft. The touch of a townsperson rather than a professional sculptor makes the story of this church warmer.

The first level has a semicircular arched portal flanked by niches, the second has a large arched window, and the third has a niche holding a statue of St. William under a curved pediment. A two-storey convent joins the church by a corridor of capiz (shell) windows set on two arches, so the side view is worth a look too.

blocks.title: Brick Bell Tower and Old Church Ruins

children.text: The octagonal brick bell tower has four levels and stands about
tall, a remnant of the old church built in the 1700s. Beside it, the fallen walls of the old church survive and hint at the earthquakes and conflicts the site has endured.

The old convent houses the Magsingal Museum, run by the National Museum. It displays the religious, agricultural and industrial tools of Ilocano life, and part of the ruins is also used as exhibit space. Opening hours change often, so check before you visit.

Starting at the church, fourteen stone Stations of the Cross are set along the town's streets. During Holy Week you can see worshippers praying along this route. If you have time, walk through town and find a few of them.

items.title: Half-Day Trip from Vigan
items.subtitle: See the church and museum, then stroll the town

children.text: Set out from the Vigan terminal or your hotel. Take a bus or jeepney bound for Ilocos Norte and ask the driver to drop you in front of Magsingal Church. The ride takes about
20–30 minutes
Start outside, looking at the facade, buttresses, bell tower and the ruins of the old church. The opposite side of the road or the edge of the yard gives a good view of all three storeys.
If the doors are open, go inside to see the mermaid-and-seashell retablo, the main altar columns and the pulpit. If Mass is under way, watch quietly from the back.
Check whether the Magsingal Museum in the old convent is open. If it is, see the Ilocano artifacts; if it is closed, ask at the parish office whether it is open.
Walk a few Stations of the Cross along the town road or look around the garden in front of the town hall, then move on to your next stop.
This route depends on local opening and Mass times. The church interior is primarily for worshippers, so keep noise down and avoid flash.

items.title: Northern Ilocos Day Trip
items.subtitle: From Vigan to Paoay and Laoag

children.text: Walk Vigan's historic district early and have breakfast.
Stop at Magsingal Church to see the retablo and the bell tower. Finish within an hour.
Keep heading north and have lunch. Travel time varies with transport and traffic, so leave some slack in a one-day plan.
Pass Paoay Church and rest in Laoag with a late lunch; if time allows, continue to the sand dunes and the coast.
Return to Laoag or Vigan for the night.
Doing this circuit by public transport alone is tight. Renting a vehicle or hiring a driver makes it much easier.
Long-distance buses such as Partas run from Manila to Vigan; sources differ on the time, so allow roughly
7–11 hours
Fares are listed anywhere from about ₱740 to ₱1,500 depending on seat class and season, so check the operator's site before booking.
From Vigan, take a bus or jeepney bound for Ilocos Norte or Laoag. Magsingal is about
from Manila.
Direct buses to Laoag often pass in front of Magsingal, but whether they stop depends on the bus, so confirm with the driver when boarding.
The nearest commercial airport is Laoag International Airport (LAO), with flights from Manila. Check the airline for current schedules.
From Laoag to Magsingal it is roughly
70 km
by map, by bus or rented car, and takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
Magsingal is about
from Vigan by the national highway.
On a bus or jeepney, remember that the church is on the highway and ask to be dropped at the church or the town hall. Confirm the exact fare locally.
You can also hire a tricycle or taxi for a round trip; the price is negotiated.
The church, bell tower, museum and town hall are all within walking distance of one another.
The Stations of the Cross run along the town roads and can be walked slowly.
Magsingal follows the Ilocos region's weather. The dry season from November to May is the most comfortable for walking, and December to February is particularly cool for visiting the church and town.

February 10 is the feast day of St. William. Feast Mass and events are held at the church around then, so it is worth timing a visit if you want the atmosphere, but check the latest announcements for the schedule and scale. During Holy Week, worshippers gather along the Way of the Cross.

Magsingal has few tourist accommodations, so most visitors stay in Vigan and come for the day. Vigan has everything from boutique stays in the historic district to inexpensive guesthouses. Staying in Laoag and coming down is also possible.

It is easiest to eat in Vigan. Ilocos specialties such as Vigan longganisa sausage, bagnet and empanada can be had at the Vigan market or around Calle Crisologo. There are also small eateries and shops along the road in Magsingal, where you can pick up simple snacks and water.
The church is a place of worship. Avoid shorts and sleeveless tops and wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees.
The retablo is high up, so a camera or phone with zoom helps you see the mermaids and shells better. Follow the church's guidance on whether photography is allowed.
Museum opening hours differ by source, with conflicting records such as Monday to Friday and by appointment only. It is wise to call or check social media before leaving Vigan.
The church's phone number is listed as (077) 726-3565, but the number may have changed, so treat it as a reference only.
Avoid sightseeing inside during Mass and look around once it has ended.
The midday sun in Ilocos is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Combining it with Vigan, Santa Maria (south) and Paoay (north) churches lets you see the Ilocos Spanish church heritage in one go.
Museum opening hours and the church's open hours change often and are described differently across sources. Check the latest information so you don't make a wasted trip.
The church interior may be closed or restricted during Mass or events.
The church is beside a highway with heavy traffic, so be careful crossing the road.
The bell tower and ruined walls are old structures, so do not enter or climb them.
Confirm public transport fares and stops locally, and agree on the fare before boarding vehicles that require bargaining.
To protect the heritage, do not touch walls or carvings and do not leave litter.
A UNESCO World Heritage city about
20–30 minutes
away by car. Its cobbled streets and Spanish-style mansions are great for walking, and lodging and restaurants are concentrated here.
A UNESCO World Heritage church in southern Ilocos Sur. Unlike Magsingal, it is a hilltop fortress-style church, so the two are interesting to compare.
Ilocos Norte's signature Baroque church, known for its massive buttresses. It fits well into an itinerary heading north.
The center of Ilocos Norte, with an airport and restaurants, and a good base for the northern itinerary.
